speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this request lor the production ol correspondence between the government and others relating to a change in reporting of the statistics of weekly steel production raises an important issue in so far as the dominion bureau of statistics is concerned, because in the final analysis the effective operation of the dominion bureau of statistics must be based on the assumption by business, unions, individuals and all organizations that all information supplied to the dominion bureau of statistics is secret and available only to the bureau.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this traditional
motion gives the opposition an opportunity to move a vote of no confidence, if it so desires, in connection with any matter concerning which the house in this session has not come to a decision.
With so much material available it is not easy to choose a particular vote of no confidence. In order to assist myself on this matter I thought it might be helpful if I looked at some of the resolutions and statements made at the recent Conservative convention, but I did not get very much help there. There was a resolution which might have been the subject for such a motion dealing with a distinctive Canadian national flag, on which the party decided that action should be taken as soon as possible, whereas our party has decided in convention that definite action on this matter is to be taken within two years of a general election.

subtopic: EFFECT OF DOUBLE DE- PRECIATION IN DEPRESSED AREAS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EFFECT OF DOUBLE DE- PRECIATION IN DEPRESSED AREAS
speechtext: When will that be?

subtopic: EFFECT OF DOUBLE DE- PRECIATION IN DEPRESSED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that, in view of the discussion of this matter in the house on Friday I thought that observation should draw some reaction from the other side. I had also hoped that perhaps at this interesting meeting we might have got some indication of the date of the forthcoming election. We did not get much enlightenment on that subject. However, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who made some strange statements indeed, according to the press said with regard to an election that "when the election does take place this is when you need workers out to sell a bill of
goods on your behalf". This is an interesting approach to a general election.
If I may, with great respect, mention this Conservative meeting, it was undoubtedly the biggest and most expensive convention ever held by the Progressive Conservative party, but from all accounts it looks as though it was about the dullest as well and the one most completely dominated by those in control of the party.

subtopic: EFFECT OF DOUBLE DE- PRECIATION IN DEPRESSED AREAS
speechtext: You are a dreamer.

subtopic: EFFECT OF DOUBLE DE- PRECIATION IN DEPRESSED AREAS
speechtext:
In that respect, and to show the contrast between the Conservative party on this side of the water and the Conservative party in Great Britain, may I quote from a reference in the London Observer of February 26 to a convention of the young Conservatives there at which a motion was moved in the following terms:
The young Conservatives deplore the unctuous terms which preface so many of the resolutions submitted to the party annual conference.
In speaking to that resolution a member of the cabinet in the United Kingdom, the secretary of state for colonial affairs, Right Hon. Iain Macleod, had this to say, and I think this certainly applies to the resolutions of this particular meeting in Ottawa so far as we have been able to see them:
The automatic and indiscriminate praise of performances which are often pedestrian is one of the dreariest features of annual conferences.

subtopic: EFFECT OF DOUBLE DE- PRECIATION IN DEPRESSED AREAS
speechtext: You are not doing badly now.

subtopic: EFFECT OF DOUBLE DE- PRECIATION IN DEPRESSED AREAS
speechtext: I think that is a very apt reference with respect to the meeting that has just finished. The president of the national Progressive Conservative association of Canada was candid enough to say over the air last night in an interview, when he was questioned about the difficulties of the rank and file of the party making themselves heard, that "we cannot have every Tom, Dick and Harry taking over".

subtopic: EFFECT OF DOUBLE DE- PRECIATION IN DEPRESSED AREAS
speechtext: Just John.

subtopic: EFFECT OF DOUBLE DE- PRECIATION IN DEPRESSED AREAS
speechtext: We were informed by the press that 200 resolutions had been sent in before the convention opened. I propose to spend the rest of my time dealing with that particular aspect of the problem on which the house has not this session taken any decision; and at the end of my reference to this particular aspect of unemployment I propose to introduce a motion that will cover that problem alone.
The governor of the Bank of Canada in his annual report had something to say on

the subject of chronic unemployment of depressed areas and the regional nature of our unemployment. He showed in that report-as indeed other authorities have shown-an awareness of the seriousness of that particular problem. The governor had this to say as found at pages 22 and 23 of his report, and this has a bearing on this problem:
Monetary expansion may play a part when it occurs in conjunction with a broad sweep of other programs of a more specific kind directed toward solving the problems in question. By itself, however, the creation of more and more money could do little toward achieving the objective.
Unemployment in Canada like economic expansion in Canada, as has so often been said in this house, has an uneven regional aspect. When there is general expansion in the country the regional incidence of unemployment is not too apparent but in years of recession or of pause, it then stands out. Since 1957 we on this side of the house have raised in this chamber this regional problem. We have pleaded for a more flexible and more selective formulation of national policies to deal with it.
The problem about which I am talking, that of chronic unemployment of depressed areas, was brilliantly analysed by Professor Judek for the Senate committee on manpower and employment in a report which he submitted to that committee on February 2 of this year. The report is entitled "Labour Surplus Market Areas". I should like to think that the Prime Minister and other hon. gentlemen opposite have studied it; but the attitude of the government toward this problem would indicate that if hon. gentlemen opposite have indeed studied it they have not accepted any of Professor Judek's recommendations to deal with it.
As a matter of fact, it is known now of course that for several sessions the attitude of the government toward this problem of depressed areas has been to deny its existence and to attack and pillory us on this side because we kept bringing it to their attention as I am attempting to do today. Then, three and half years after the election and three and half months after the announcement by the Minister of Finance last December that the government was going to take some action, they brought in some regulations. We were told that these regulations were designed to meet this particular problem. Presumably they are a part of that massive attack on unemployment to which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) referred to the other day, an attack so massive that there are still 700,000 or more Canadians in this country suffering from unemployment.
However, the government announcement which I believe was made last December and the government regulations brought in by

the Minister of Labour a few days ago do indicate at least some recognition that the problem does at least exist. Hon. gentlemen opposite must have not discarded their blinkers but-and we can take some satisfaction out of this

they are beginning at last to look around them. They have stopped denying that there is any chronic unemployment to attack; and so we have these government proposals which could have been brought in by order in council any time since last December, notwithstanding what the Minister of Finance has said about this matter. We on this side of the house have already stated our opinion about these regulations. We consider them to be ludicrously inadequate, confused and restrictive.
In these regulations the responsibility for initiating action looking toward assistance has been abdicated by the government-we were told the other day in the name of democracy-and turned over to the municipalities themselves. From what we heard the other day, presumably it was humiliating for the government to designate an area as an area of surplus labour or a depressed area. It was not humiliating for similar action to be taken by the democractic governments of the United Kingdom, the United States, France, Scandinavia and Belgium. In this country presumably we are in this respect more democratic.
Under these regulations the government says to an area or a municipality, in effect: designate yourself, if you so desire, as depressed and then we will decide, by attempting to apply our inadequate criteria, whether you really are depressed and are to receive any special help under these regulations. If not, you are a self-designated depressed area and without help from us. If the municipalities go through this preliminary stage of designating themselves as depressed areas and submitting themselves to the examination of the government in respect of its criteria, what help will they receive under these regulations?
Here is where the labouring mountain really brought forth an abortive mouse. We on this side have already pointed out in this house that the criteria concerned are uncertain, confused and restrictive. They deal with areas having under 10,000 workers and with areas having over 10,000 workers. As far as the first category is concerned the regulations will be quite unworkable because the statistics required over the period in question, which I believe is eight years, are not readily available. If we are wrong in this matter will the Minister of Labour or some other minister-we do not even know which minister will be responsible for this matter- tell us how these regulations will be applied

to this particular situation and where and how, if he is trying to apply the regulations, the minister will get the detailed information required for the eight years.
As far as communities of over 10,000 are concerned the regulations are obvious and excessively rigid and inflexible. They cover a period of eight years, four of which were ones of great expansion. To qualify under these circumstances a region must have had 6 per cent or 7 per cent of unemployment during 36 of the 48 summer months and employment must have actually declined during that period. These regulations are startling in their contrast with those adopted in other countries which earlier have recognized and tried to do something about the situation, particularly the United Kingdom and the United States of America, the senate of which passed a very important bill dealing with this matter on Friday of last week, I think. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, these regulations have very little relationship to these criteria suggested by Professor Judek at page 532 of his report, and which we would commend to the government as being much more helpful and effective for depressed areas.
If you do qualify under this criteria what help do you get? You get double depreciation for a new industry moving into a depressed area for one year only, one of the first three years.

What kind of help do the designated depressed areas in the country get under these regulations? As I pointed out, they get double depreciation for one year only of the first three, this help to apply only if a new industry makes substantial profits over one of the first three years, something which is not likely in that period of time in a depressed area. The tax reductions during that one year are to be offset later by higher taxes. That is the situation, Mr. Speaker, so far as help to the depressed areas of this country is concerned. These minor, uncertain, illusory tax benefits are supposed to be an incentive for manufacturers to move into a depressed area. It is no wonder that on March 18 the Financial Post wrote as follows:
We find it difficult to believe that the government could seriously consider the new regulation as a genuine tax incentive.
Indeed, these new regulations are a farce in so far as they are a part of that massive attack on unemployment that the Minister of Labour talked about. Oh, they may have some use. We hope they may attract some industry into the depressed areas, if those depressed areas can meet these confused and restrictive criteria; but as to being a massive attack on unemployment, they do not make sense. Perhaps the Prime Minister or some member of his cabinet will tell us how much work is likely to be created in this period of high unemployment by this kind of regulation which has been described in these terms by the Financial Post.
I will put another paragraph from the Financial Post on record. It reads:
We will not be surprised if the new regulatiot provides more employment in the civil service ir. Ottawa than it does in the depressed areas of the country.
Let the Minister of Trade and Commerce rub his hands, put on his cheerleader's hat and give us a pep talk on this governmental triumph, this massive attack on unemployment. What we need, Mr. Speaker, is something a little more impressive than this kind of sham attack.
Leaving out general policies created for expansion, which would affect the depressed areas-but I would be out of order if I talked about them, Mr. Speaker-may I mention

what we think are the special measures which should be taken at this time for this special problem? Not all of these matters can be applied in the same way to all areas of surplus labour. At our convention in January, when we dealt with these matters, we said this and I quote from the resolution:
A new Liberal government would co-operate with provinces and municipalities in providing tax incentives to encourage industries to locate in such areas.
This is not the kind of miniscule tax incentive which is in these regulations in their present form.

I will begin to do that if my hon. friend will possess his soul in patience. I go on to read from our resolution:
It would see that more credit is available to business in these areas. It would help to finance power, transport and other basic economic developments. Through programs for urban and rural rehabilitation, it would see that both credit for private business and money for public improvement are readily available.
On July 29, 1960 I had this to say in the House of Commons, as reported at page 7320 of Hansard:
If we want as a nation to deal effectively with the employment problem and at the same time to minimize the expenditure of public funds, we must arrive at a regional formulation of certain national policies, and in order to arrive at such a formulation we must know in greater detail and much more concretely than we do now the different structures and the peculiar behaviour of our economic regions.
We have made proposals in this house, Mr. Speaker. We made them on May 3, 1960, in 1959 and in 1958 to deal with this question of chronic unemployment in depressed areas. I am going to sum up the position we have taken over recent years in this matter by putting these proposals on Hansard at this time in the form of a six-point program for areas of chronic and serious unemployment:
1. An area rehabilitation agency should be set up within the federal government to implement, in co-operation with provincial and local authorities, an over-all program of economic assistance to the depressed areas of our country. That agency of the federal government should designate under the responsibility of the federal government such areas on the basis of suitable criteria and carry out detailed and concrete studies of their economies. The criteria for this purpose would not be these of the regulations put forward by the Minister of Labour which in our view do not go far enough, but would be much closer to the criteria laid down in the report of Professor Judek.
Labour Conditions
2.	A flexible fiscal policy should be adapted to the specific needs of those areas which may require special encouragement to develop their primary resources, to establish new secondary manufacturing industries, to improve their transportation facilities or to increase their export trade.
To be more specific on this point, Mr. Speaker, such a flexible policy could include
(a)	capital grants for development, such as the Atlantic provinces development fund, which we have advocated for some time;
(b)	tax incentives such as temporary tax exemptions or concessions for distressed areas, to apply not only to new industries moving in, but to the expansion and modernization of industries already in the areas;
(c)	special consideration for distressed areas in public works programs; (d) special consideration for such areas in winter works programs, with the federal share of the cost extended to include cost of materials as well as labour costs.
3.	Easier credit facilities should be made available to depressed areas. For that purpose the industrial development bank should be separated from the Bank of Canada and operated vigorously to provide capital assistance for depressed areas, a proposal which we have made time and time again inside and outside the house.
4.	Special training and retraining programs should be implemented in order to prepare the workers displaced by declining industry for new or expanding industries. These programs should be closely related to the requirements of redevelopment projects and unemployed persons should be given allowances for these retraining programs.
5.	Special urban renewal measures should be implemented to clear blighted areas for new industry or housing, with a municipal development fund set up to facilitate the financing of the municipal share of these measures. The federal government should increase from the present 50 per cent level its share in the cost of clearing blighted areas in depressed regions for any appropriate use, whether it be for housing, commerce, industry, transport or for open spaces. It should extend its contribution to cover the cost of renewing and improving basic services such as water, sewers and streets in the redeveloped areas.
6.	The rural development program proposed by the Senate committee on land use in 1960 should be closely integrated with the over-all national policy for depressed areas.
I believe that this six-point program is desirable, comprehensive and responsible. It recognizes-as other countries such as the United Kingdom, the United States, France, Belgium and the Scandinavian countries have

Labour Conditions
already recognized-that the problem of depressed areas is a special one and requires special treatment adapted, of course, to Canadian needs and conditions. It is in line with the recommendations made by experts in this field such as Professor Judek whom I have mentioned and Professor Cairncross of the United Kingdom. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, it is significant that Professor Cairncross, a well known British economist, who was appointed by the present Minister of Forestry, (Mr. Flemming) and the other premiers of the Atlantic provinces to make a study of the economic problems of that region, has come out in his report with two major proposals which we on this side of the house made over a year ago. The first one has to do with the encouragement of secondary manufacturing industries through tax incentives, which I mentioned again this afternoon, and the other envisages the reorientation of the industrial development bank for regional purposes, which I also mentioned this afternoon. So I hope that during this discussion the Minister of Forestry will tell us what he now thinks of those proposals.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the proposals I have made are supported by the presentation made by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities to the Senate committee on manpower and employment on February 15 of this year, I believe. It is supported also by the Atlantic provinces economic council. We on this side believe-and we reiterate our belief which we have expressed many times- that such a program as this one is needed in Canada at this present time of unemployment emergency. We also believe that the measures implemented by the government to assist in the solution of this problem, the regulations already brought down by the government as a solution to the problem are unworkable and too restrictive and that they will be ineffective. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to move, seconded by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that the provision for double depreciation announced last December will prove ineffective in dealing with the problems of depressed areas, and regrets that the government has imposed the responsibility for the designation of such areas on the municipalities, and that the definition of depressed areas is too restrictive."

The people who paid for the party will be making the resolutions and they will be accepted as policies. There will be no equivocation about whether any resolution represents exactly the policy of the new party. We will take these resolutions as representing our policies. I suggest too that these policies will be decided upon by people who have been sitting in living rooms over the last two years discussing, thinking and reacting to the problems of Canadian politics. The session of the house may not be over in July but I hope that it will be over and that hon. members will remain in Ottawa because we invite all of you to come and watch a real political rally in action here in the city of Ottawa. I can assure you that no matter what the gentlemen of the press have to say about the rally they will not say it is uninteresting.
I note, Mr. Speaker, that some hon. members including the Prime Minister are still talking about free enterprise and doctrinaire socialism. I hope that this will be one of the things we will try to bring into focus before the Canadian people next July. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we have need in Canada to talk about these things. I must admit, though, I find it rather difficult to understand what our friends to the left mean by planning with a capital "P". After the convention was over I noticed that somebody was asked if they expected the leaders of business to lose any initiative because of this planning. He said, no. Just how you plan from the bottom, I am not quite sure. Nevertheless, this is evidently to be the plan. May I say that next July you will have a real party of the left; and let me assure you that plenty will be heard from this political sector in the near future.
I was rather concerned, too, about the fact that our friends to the left found themselves in a dilemma in British Columbia, However, I am sure the rules would not allow me to go into that aspect of their policy, as a result of which they divided and supported a bill which negated the political rights of a large section of the people.

The last few months have been an incredible experience for all of us. Last November when we came here we expected this government would make an all-out attack on unemployment. After we arrived we discovered that really there had merely been a change in the timetable and we were only here six weeks earlier because this session was not concerned with unemployment at allin fact, the word "unemployment" was not to be mentioned. We discovered in November that the government was quite willing to put through a number of long term measures. We have congratulated the government upon their measure connected with loans to small businesses and upon their housing policy. However, what we on this side of the house expected was an immediate attack upon unemployment, one which would drastically reduce the number of people who were unemployed. I am afraid we cannot congratulate the government upon this feature of their policy.
One snowy evening last December we came into this house expecting to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) give us some hope. We thought possibly some gigantic expansion of the public sector would be revealed. We expected some unusual tax cuts in order to give the people of this nation greater purchasing power. What did we find? We found very little, merely this double depreciation for one year to new industries moving into areas in which there are a number of people unemployed. By this time we were grasping at straws. We waited and hoped that this measure would do something for those areas in which the people today are living without much hope. We waited. I am reminded by this thought that about an hour ago spring came to Canada. Winter is over. It is too bad that winter unemployment cannot be over, too. Winter is over, and the government has survived. However, unemployment remains. There has been no storming of the ramparts by those who are on relief. So far as this government is concerned they have survived the winter.
However, as I have said, we waited and grasped at this straw hoping that it would do something for those areas in which unemployment was chronic. We waited with patience from December 3 until March 2 in the hope that some announcement would be made which would enable us to go back to our constituents and say, "See what the government of Canada is going to do in order to move industry into this area and in order to create a growing, healthy economy." On March 2 the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) did rise in his place and reveal that this delay was unnecessary. There was no reason for this delay because there was no real problem to
Labour Conditions
be solved. However, by this time the government had conceded that unemployment was present. During the early part of the winter the government did not regard unemployment as very serious; indeed, in their view there was no crisis at all.
On March 2 we discovered that in areas of over 10,000 which had had considerable unemployment during the summer months from 1953 onward, some help would be given and in areas in which the labour force was under 10,000 certain other measures had been suggested. These areas will be called surplus manpower areas. Certainly, this description, "surplus manpower areas" is ironic. Distressed areas are out of the picture and the term "depressed areas" is unacceptable. We call them "surplus manpower areas". I am certainly glad to know that at least one government on this continent is willing to call a spade a spade. I believe that when we call these areas "surplus manpower areas", we are only adding to the confusion.
When the Minister of Labour rose to outline his method for reducing unemployment I noticed that he gave us a few examples. I believe mention was made of Elliot Lake, Springhill and some places in Cape Breton. However, not a single secondary manufacturing area was mentioned. I would suggest that this is perhaps one of the most serious lacks in this particular policy. What is so magical about 1953? Is everyone in Canada who is receiving unemployment insurance benefits dated back to 1953 suddenly going to disappear? I do not believe so. Why do we talk about 1953? Surely this government realizes that in a secondary manufacturing area you can have an immediate crisis resulting from a simple change in trading policy or from some technological change. The whole manpower situation can be quickly changed.
I could suggest that in the city of Peterborough, for example, there was considerable employment in 1957; that is nearly four years ago. We are now going back to 1953, a time when there was absolutely no unemployment whatever in many areas now suffering. I suggest that the measure advocated by the minister takes no account whatever of the particular problems of secondary manufacturing areas such as Windsor and Cornwall. It does not take into account the different kinds of unemployment. Why do we turn to the summer months? Does this government believe the only real problem is seasonal unemployment? Does the government believe you need not worry about what happens in the winter as long as you can get by? We realize that seasonal unemployment is here, but it is only a very small part of this problem.

Labour Conditions
In many areas, there is the matter of structural unemployment. There have been tremendous changes in the uses of certain products. There have been great trade differences. As a result of these things, you have a large number of unemployed emerging very quickly. The emergence of this large number probably goes no farther back than 1958 or 1959. The measure put forward by the minister takes no account of one of the main causes of unemployment, as a result of technological change; I refer to the problem of automation. This problem has been developing for a small number of years. Indeed, the developments that have taken place in Peterborough in two years have been tremendous and have had a tremendous effect upon the labouring force.
I would suggest that the selection of 1953 as some kind of magical date is unrealistic and unacceptable. The government waits until spring comes, and I suppose we shall soon be into the summer. I am wondering what will happen. I suppose the government is hoping that summer employment will bring a measure of relief. I would suggest, as did the Leader of the Opposition, that we are not out of the woods as yet, even though 1960 might be a better year economically. If the trends of the last 10 years continue, we shall have more unemployment within another two or three years. One does not have to be an expert economist to know that this government has done nothing to ensure that this cyclical unemployment will be alleviated.
I certainly feel the greatest sympathy for the unemployed individual. The cost of his food remains high. His rent has not gone down as it did during the depression in the thirties. Surely he is becoming more disillusioned, Surely he is coming to the point where he must really face the freedom of being unemployed, of seeing his home disappearing, of seeing his family hopes and the hopes of his young people slowly "going down the drain", to put it in the vernacular. I certainly hope these young people who are here today do not judge democracy, democratic action and the possibilities of democracy by what this government has done during the past six months.
This is what the government has left us with and we are very much disgusted with it. Any city or municipality must come to this government in order to reap the benefits of double depreciation and can do so only after that area has been established as a depressed area through the research and statistics of the area itself. This surely is a matter of some considerable concern. Surely this is something that the Department of Labour should do on the basis of unemployment in 1961 rather

than on the basis of unemployment in 1953 in those areas having a surplus of manpower. We feel that this is one area in which the government should accept its responsibility, for what exists now, to an even greater extent than it does through this small and inadequate double depreciation program. We feel that this program will not be sufficient in terms of what must eventually be done. It is the view of this group in the corner that unemployment is a serious problem requiring a direct approach rather than an indirect one.
With regard to what private business can do in this regard,-and I think it has done very much during many years-it is the opinion of our group in this corner that private business does not have the power of an over-all approach to deal with this problem. We feel indeed that private business would prosper under the circumstances that we suggest. We feel it is time for a direct approach and for dealing directly through government agencies with the problem of unemployment.
I am not going to reiterate the things which have been suggested by members of the C.C.F. party. One has only to look in Hansard to see them. However, Mr. Speaker, I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West, that the following should be accepted as a subamendment to the amendment put forward by the Leader of the Opposition:
and, furthermore, this house is of the opinion that the government should promptly implement additional measures to immediately stimulate employment and the further growth of our economy.

Mr. Speaker, the various debates on unemployment which have taken place in this house during the present session have only served to reveal a sad state of affairs in its naked ugliness. This is a continuous problem without continuous measures to meet it. The measures which have been advanced so far by the government have failed to meet the situation.
Labour Conditions
The criteria to be used in order for a municipality to qualify for double depreciation only under certain circumstances is not only unworkable but absolutely restrictive, as pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition.
In my own constituency unemployment has been creeping up at an alarming rate from a registered unemployment figure of 2,600 in November of 1960 to 4,300 according to the latest figures available. The lakehead district is now classed by the federal Department of Labour as a substantial labour surplus area. It is one of 22 communities with a labour force of between 25,000 and 75,000, so designated across the country. It can be said, without much fear of successful contradiction, that although the problem of chronic unemployment is probably more severe in Canada than in any other western nation, no nation has done less to cope with it.
Several years ago when Britain was confronted with a similar situation, the government of that country did not hesitate to launch a mass attack on areas of unemployment with a high degree of success.
The double depreciation measure announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) last December in the baby budget can hardly be classed as a great inducement to establish a new industry in a depressed area; and according to the only interpretation possible for the formula only a few areas can qualify. In other words my own constituency, because it has only in the last two or three years fallen on hard times due to unemployment, is thus by-passed.
The winter works program, while it has been of some help, has not fulfilled expectations. For one thing it has ignored the difficulties of the municipalities to finance needed projects which would employ a considerable labour force. It is indeed regrettable that it did not include participation in the cost of materials to be used in these projects. Until the government establishes a municipal loan fund, which I have advocated in this house at every opportunity, the extended municipal winter works program will not make any appreciable dent in the ranks of the unemployed.
The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities has long been on record as favouring a federal-municipal loan fund and in its submission to the government on February 7, 1958, it urged that such a fund be established. I wish to emphasize the fact that such a fund has been specifically requested and has received unqualified support across the country from the municipal governments. Moreover, nearly all the provincial premiers are on record as endorsing a municipal loan fund.

Labour Conditions
In recent years local governments have been pratically forced to stand aside and allow all senior levels of government and private industry to gobble up nearly all the available supply of money. To finance the most necessary and urgent needs, such as schools, sewers, water mains, hospitals, paved streets, parks and recreational facilities, local governments have had to borrow at excessive rates of interest and it has often been difficult to obtain funds in Canada, thus forcing municipal governments to borrow in New York and helping to create the unnatural rise in the value of the Canadian dollar, with a detrimental effect on our exports.

We are trying to advance suggestions in order to promote work in depressed areas such as my constituency and all others as well. The theme of the conference to which I have referred embraces in a single phrase one of the fundamentals necessary to put us back on the road to employment and prosperity. An expanding economy, which we need in order to get rid of the depressed areas, demands more capital investment and judicious handling of tariffs.

Nothing less than an all-out effort will do. The time for half measures is past. We are living in a day and age of technological change which has taken place in our factories and our industries, on our railroads and even on our farms. The result has been a steady increase in unemployment. This is one of the factors, among others, which has contributed to our dilemma. It has contributed to the condition of the depressed areas with which we are dealing at this moment.
This is the time for the government to step in and make a study of technological developments in every industry. This would not necessarily mean interfering with private industry, but I do think that sudden changes affecting employment should be handled intelligently and with a sense of humanity. Having this in mind, the government would be well advised to ask industry to inform it before industry employs methods that will displace a large number of employees because of automation, and competent advisers should be called in at once in an effort to find an immediate alternative in the form of work for these displaced persons.
Canadians have supported in the past-and they will do so in the future-programs for the alleviation of suffering in many parts of the world, especially in underdeveloped regions. We have always done so out of sympathy as well as in the national interest. I cannot believe that Canada will not support reasonable programs for the unemployed of the nation, be they victims of a disaster or victims of technological change. Technological changes are another reason why we have depressed areas in our country. The Minister of Labour has indicated that his department is undertaking a detailed study of the problem in the railway industry brought about by automation and technological changes and that the study is similar to that being made by the royal commission investigating the automobile industry. If it takes the experts as long to look into the railway problem as it has taken them in the case of the automobile industry, this will mean that the situation on the railways will get much worse before we can expect any action from the government.

It is only by the determination of the Canadian people who are willing to sacrifice some of their own comforts that this problem will be remedied. I believe that the remedying of this situation will require a great deal of thought and effective action, and particularly leadership by this government of a stronger nature than the introduction of double depreciation for depressed areas. I admit that there is no easy solution to this very complicated and involved problem which is a product of the free enterprise system. The Prime Minister stated that the free enterprise system was going to be supported during the next election by his party as against the socialist approach of this party. The Prime Minister is on the defensive in this respect because the blight is one of the effects of the free enterprise system.
We in this group offer democratic socialism not as an overnight cure but as a philosophical approach to life that will remedy this cyclical unemployment. I recognize that we live in a democracy. In a dictatorship problems can be cured by edict and by order. Dictators do not need to wait for the consent of the people. A dictator could put all the people in Canada to work tomorrow. However, in a democracy you have to recognize the parliamentary institutions; you have to recognize the democratic principles. What you do must have the consent of the people as a whole; otherwise it is not effective.
What we criticize is the failure of the government to give leadership at this time, beyond this question of double depreciation and other long term measures which are fully justified but which will not remedy the situation in the near future. In contrast to this suggestion of double depreciation and the designation of certain areas as depressed areas, we suggest the way to meet this prob-blem is a program of long term and short term arrangements. We believe that long term arrangements, as opposed to this piecemeal double depreciation program, will require a conscious effort of planning by the people as a whole instead of leaving the planning of our economy to fewer and fewer corporations whose boards of directors decide whether or not men shall be employed. This planning will require co-operation between governments, between industry and labour, between labour and agriculture and other segments of our population.
This planning is only possible with the acceptance of a totally different approach to life, a different social and economic philosophy. In this way governments can influence

the direction of investment rather than have, as I believe we have had in recent years, direction by boards of directors without any relationship to what was happening in the other provinces with respect to the development of our natural resources. We could then bring these resources into production as the result of a plan rather than have them brought into production as the result of a decision of a board of directors located in New York or somewhere like that, and without any thought given to whether or not we are exhausting our natural resources or developing them at too rapid a rate. An overall plan would provide for the education of our young people, the retraining of our older people and the rehabilitation of the disabled. Some of these things are mentioned in measures that have been introduced by the government. These are long term plans that would take some time to have effect. This planning with respect to the development of markets over the years is very necessary indeed, as is long term planning with respect to research into the economics and the development of natural resources, the use of fiscal policies and so on.
We are urging this suggestion, in general, as a long term plan in opposition to the program advanced by the government with respect to double depreciation. What about the short term program? We must do something that will have an effect in the near future. People cannot remain unemployed year after year without their morale being destroyed. I can tell you right now that I have no sympathy for the lazy man. There are malingerers in all groups in society. Since there is a small percentage of people in any group who will take advantage of any type of legislation, we find that fact is emphasized. We do not talk about the malingering of the corporations who have obtained concessions valued at millions of dollars as a result of incorrect statements, and so on.
We suggest a long term program as opposed to this short term double depreciation program. We suggest there is an opportunity for long term loans and aid to underdeveloped countries at low interest rates. We suggest this will provide outlets for our industrial and agricultural surpluses while at the same time providing increased employment and production. Is it not better to keep our workers working constantly and our farmers producing and paying income tax than to have the present-day rate of unemployment? Think of all the income tax that is lost on account of unemployment. This loss must amount to hundreds of millions of dollars each year, and it results directly from the lack of markets for our 90205-6-199J

The government of this country represents all the people, and the wealth of Canada in the abstract belongs to the people of Canada. The government borrows not as companies do, but on the capacity of the total Canadian population to produce. We suggest the government of Canada could use the national credit to a much greater extent by permitting public investment programs for highways, hospitals, schools and public utilities instead of just providing this very minute remedy of double depreciation.
In the proposal for double depreciation it is suggested that it will have a benefit overnight and that companies would locate in certain places immediately. Companies do not establish industries in locations because of double depreciation or employment surpluses, but fundamentally because of the nearness of resources and the relationship between the factory, transportation and markets. These things are all taken into consideration when a company locates and it will take possibly a year or two before these companies get into operation. In the meantime this double depreciation program will have no effect so far as reducing the number of unemployed is concerned.
In addition to this double depreciation measure we suggest that the government undertake a national investment program for the utilization of the nationally unemployed, the utilization of idle natural resources, and the utilization of idle national credit at this time.

Up to this date we have heard very little from the Atlantic premiers in this regard.
It has been said on many occasions, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government, which is called upon to spend $1 out of every $5 the country produces, can be considered as the biggest business in Canada. It is also recognized that in a country with such a diverse economy and such diverse interests it is the responsibility of the federal government to give consideration to all sectors of the economy, to all classes of people and to all regions of the country, and in doing so it must implement policies that are in the national interest. The function of the federal government is to create that kind of economic climate in which private enterprise and, more so, private initiative can spearhead the development of every region and where the national growth of the country can be shared on an equal basis by all areas and not be centralized to the benefit of preferred sections of the country.

It is most unfortunate that, on every occasion when we on the opposition side are attempting to bring forward constructive ideas, when we are urging the government to take bold and comprehensive measures to cope with the existing situation, we are accused, as we have heard in the last few days, of dredging up gloom; and of spreading talk of depression; and members on the other side even go so far as to say that we are holding the Canadian people by fear. It is most unfortunate that those to whom has been assigned the responsibility of government should be the first ones to dodge their responsibility and to try to lay the responsibility for events that happen on the shoulders of past administrations or the present opposition.
Is it the fault of the opposition, Mr. Speaker, if the unemployment figures which will be released tomorrow or the next day will show close to 800,000 unemployed in this country? Is it the fault of the opposition if those figures will be the highest in the history of Canada since the hungry 30's? I might also ask, is it the fault of the opposition if the unemployment insurance fund, a fund which was over $900 million when this government took office, is at the moment I am speaking under $200 million?
In supporting the amendment introduced by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon, it is my intention to deal with three main aspects affecting the Atlantic provinces and it is my hope that this time hon. members on the government side, particularly those from the Atlantic region, will refrain from personal abuse such as we have heard in the house on recent occasions. If our suggestions are sound and are of a constructive nature, those same hon. members would be well advised and would serve the interest of their constituents to better advantage if they would use their personal good will and their good influence to have the government of the day implement those measures which would benefit the Atlantic region and restore our economy in line with the rest of the country.
It is the duty of the government, we all know, to initiate immediate and bold action to take care of the chronic unemployment problems which we have to admit are growing worse and worse. The situation as we see it now may not adjust itself with the melting of the snow, and the coming of spring, which in fact started this afternoon, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) suggested to the house last year. The measures introduced so far have been inadequate, insufficient and incapable of meeting the serious problem of unemployment. Since taking office the government has been reluctant to face 90205-6-200

In his address Mr. Johnson deplored the fact that the unemployment problem is more critical ii? the Atlantic region than in any other region in Canada. He described the Atlantic region as largely a primary producer for the country and, he said, one which gets no benefit from the national tariff policy and one which bears far more than its share of the cost of the national transportation system.
The Atlantic region, Mr. Speaker, is an area with surplus manpower, an area where the percentage of the labour force without jobs and seeking work is at all times much higher than the Canadian average and in certain periods almost 100 per cent higher. The Atlantic region as a whole should be considered as an area where there has been a substantial increase of continued unemployment over the years and an area which would qualify under this program without having to be subjected to the strict definition given by the Minister of Labour. Every time we put forward such proposals with sincerity and in the hope that the government would accept them or at least give some of these suggestions favourable consideration, we were subjected to the same type of personal abuse as that to which I was subjected in the house. I was accused of being ignorant and even of adopting a hypocritical attitude. Even if it is now almost too late, I still urge this government to explore the need for economic development in the mining areas of Cape Breton and to study the possibility of producing coal as a more competitive source of energy. Once again I urge this government to undertake at once, without further delay, the establishment of a committee of practical men to whom will be given the task of finding new industries that might replace that part of the mining industry which would be displaced by the mine closures. On the average, unemployment in the Atlantic regions is just about 50 per cent higher than it is in Canada as a whole. In certain periods of the year and in some particular sections, it reaches a figure as much as 100 per cent higher than the national average. Not only must the Atlantic region be recognized as an area for double depreciation under the program advocated by the government, but the remedy offered is not adequate and will not produce satisfactory results.
APEC is calling for bold new policies in an area where the economy is weak and where unemployment threatens to remain greater than in any other part of Canada unless bold new policies are developed without delay. APEC, in its determination to solve this problem, has been able to develop such unity in economic thinking as to determine that secondary manufacturing industries alone based on local and other resources could create the 107,000 job openings which will be required in the next 20 years to bring employment in the Atlantic area up to the national average. APEC has suggested a formula which, if implemented, could substantially close the present gap of approximately 22,000 jobs which are required in the Atlantic region in order to enable that region to share on an equal basis with the rest of Canada.
From APEC's program issued a month ago today, on February 20 of this year, may I be permitted to quote briefly as follows:
The profit climate here, therefore, must be made sufficiently attractive to investors in secondary manufacturing industry to induce them to locate in the region. To this end, APEC recommends the adoption of fiscal policies having specific application to lagging regions as distinct from pinpointed distressed areas. They should also differ from policies applying to the nation as a whole in that they should have particular application to the needs of sub-average regions of which the Atlantic constitutes one.
APEC is prepared to work with responsible taxing authorities to arrive at a satisfactory formula and makes the adoption of such regional fiscal policies a major goal. It proposes a continuing study of such policies in all their aspects. Such fiscal policies should include, among other things, (a) regional tax and investment allowances and (b) accelerated

depreciation, both to be available for a stated and suitable period to permit sound business planning.
This plan, Mr. Speaker, is quite different from the double depreciation for one year which is now offered in the government's program. Before discussing further the proposals offered in this well prepared program, may I be permitted to comment briefly on the two main points offered for consideration. The first suggestion calls for regional tax and investment allowances. No such offer is contained in the present double depreciation program announced in the baby budget of December 20, 1960. I recognize that the tax incentive to business enterprises included in the baby budget is at least of some significance to the Atlantic provinces where the number of small businesses is relatively high, but it is far from being enough.
May I be allowed to point out in passing that the benefits under this measure will apply largely to firms which have passed their initial development stage and are already in the profit making stage. What is requested and what is needed is a regional tax and investment allowance or, in other words, a regional tax incentive which would induce small secondary industries to establish in the area under opportunities equal to those offered in the more populated areas where the chances of success guarantee a larger measure of security. If the economy of the Atlantic provinces is to be subjected to unusual strains, if the Atlantic position is determined by recognized factors which cause such differences with the rest of Canada, then we must take it for granted that measures must be implemented which will restrain or narrow the gap which is causing such a situation to the detriment of certain segments of our population and, I would add, to the detriment of our general economy. Not only is the per capita investment relatively low in the region, but the average total investment is directed to a greater extent to those sectors where it provides limited employment. In other words it is directed in large proportion to non-business investment thus providing limited and temporary employment for a limited period only. What is required is inducement and incentive for investment in our primary and secondary industries. This is not provided for in the proposal which the government now has before us.
The three primary occupations which have played an important role in the economy of the Atlantic provinces are farming, fishing, and lumbering or logging. Statistics will show that the maritime employment in agriculture alone has dropped about 50 per cent since 1940, and in the lumber and wood industry by approximately 45 per cent. Only in the 90205-6-200J
Labour Conditions
fishing and fish processing industry has employment remained fairly constant.
The problems of agriculture, as they affect the eastern provinces, are presently receiving attention in the consideration of the estimates of that particular department. I should like to point out at this time that the fishing and fish processing industry also occupies an important position in the economy of the Atlantic provinces and should be considered seriously under this program.
In the post-war period there has been increased activity in the building of modern fishing vessels and processing plants. Here again there is room for improvement and expansion, and here again we see an opportunity for the application of a policy of regional tax and investment allowances. In the construction of fishing vessels alone, the federal government has not varied one iota in its policy since 1946, which is 15 years ago. The construction of fishing vessels alone is an important factor as a source of employment in the Atlantic region. I am one of those individuals who believe in the expansion and modernization of our fishing fleet. Large quantities of fish are in our waters, but large quantities are caught by foreign ships and, in many cases, taken to Europe to be processed and reshipped to this continent. We in the Atlantic region can increase our production and our sales, and can produce additional employment for our unemployed. Sound expansion will require larger boats, modernization of equipment, and a larger market or outlet particularly on this continent.
A system of investment allowances should be introduced which would also apply to trawlers or draggers built in Canadian yards. I believe in Canadian built ships because I want to keep our Canadian shipyards in operation, and I am convinced that our Canadian shipyards and workers are qualified to do the job and do it right. I admit that the cost of construction will be higher than that for ships built in foreign yards, but this is where the government should intervene with a regional tax and investment allowance policy and, when necessary, with substantial grants in order to allow our producers to compete with foreign built trawlers. The opportunity is here for the Atlantic provinces to increase employment and to bring to our region each year additional millions of dollars of new wealth which could be distributed to fishermen and shore help alike.
The government of this country is missing the boat in not recognizing the possibilities of development of our fishing industry. The Atlantic provinces are doing their share to promote this vital industry but the financial resources at their disposal are too limited

Labour Conditions
to reach the goal which they would like to attain. Is it logical that the fishing industry today, outside of technical assistance and advice provided by the Department of Fisheries, should be operating on the same basis as that which was established, as I said earlier as far back as 1946, and with the same measure of assistance? Again I could be called to order if I attempted to elaborate on this most important factor of our maritime economy, but may I be allowed to ask the government if it is logical to be granting today, under the present high cost of construction, the same subsidy of $165 a ton on the construction of fishing vessels of the dragger or long-liner type when in 1946 or 1947 a 60-foot dragger cost in the vicinity of $30,000 against a cost of $60,000 today for a similar boat?
As I said earlier in my remarks, APEC has set the requirement of a depressed area. If the government does not want to accept their definition may I be allowed to say that not only has APEC set the requirements of a double depreciation area but it has shown that the Atlantic region, with unemployment rates 5 per cent above the national average, needs now 22,000 new jobs, and that the main source for the provision of such jobs relies on the development of secondary industry.
Before reaching the third and last point of my remarks concerning Atlantic problems, I should like to stress the importance of concentrating on a type of investment which has greater ability for providing continuing employment. I am not against investment in housing, public buildings or others, but I urge the government to give particular consideration to the type of investment and the type of public projects which could help in providing continuing employment in such depressed areas as the Atlantic provinces. I have in mind particularly the improvement of harbour facilities for fishing and shipping purposes.
In my own constituency of Gloucester improvements are required for the port of Bathurst. Such improvements would be beneficial to existing industry and would lead to further expansion and increased production of our natural resources. In other areas such as Maisonnette, Lower Caraquet, and Pigeon Hill, improvements to landing and docking facilities would result automatically in increased fish production, additional employment and increased revenue for the communities concerned. Those are the types of investment which should be of concern to the government. Improved shipping or transportation facilities, to the benefit of existing natural resources, and such projects as the Chignecto canal, are the types of investment which should concern the federal government. They are the types of investment in capital projects which should

receive priority in the government's program in its willingness to meet the problems and the needs of the Atlantic region.
I have now reached that part of my remarks which will deal with a study sponsored by the Atlantic provinces research board. This study was referred to very briefly this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition when he made reference to the proposals offered by Professor A. K. Cairncross in his report "Economic Development and the Atlantic Provinces".
In the introduction to his report, which I now have before me, Mr. Cairncross discloses the purpose of his study and describes the terms of reference of his proposed survey. I will not take up the time of the house by going into the detail of those terms of reference. In the first part of his report Mr. Cairncross deals first with the monetary policy and its effects on the economy of the Atlantic region, and in the second part he refers to the problems of regional economic development for an area where the economy lags behind that of the rest of Canada.
It may be noted here that Mr. Cairncross has fully recognized the position of the Atlantic provinces and the significant disparities which call for special measures from the federal government level. In other words, he did not have to use the restrictive and unworkable criteria suggested by the Minister of Labour to determine that the Atlantic region must be accepted as an area requiring appropriate policies.
He certainly did not shift the initial responsibility to municipalities and he did not hesitate to suggest on the part of the federal government more flexible and selective policies which in his judgment should be applied to the Atlantic region without any doubt or hesitation.
In reviewing the effect of monetary policy on the economy of the Atlantic provinces Mr. Cairncross admitted that a large part of the flow of credit into private investments comes, not from private but from public institutions. In his opinion there is nothing in the nature of things obliging these institutions to charge a uniform rate of interest on their loans or to make credit available on similar terms to all borrowers. He states in one section of his report:
If money is tight elsewhere in Canada, the Atlantic provinces cannot be completely sheltered from the consequences merely by a decision on the part of the banks to go on lending in that area as before.
This is very significant to the economic development of the Atlantic provinces.
In summarizing his remarks on monetary policy he added these words, which are to be found on page 6 of his report:

I should like to make one further general comment. "Tight money" is an intermittent phenomenon and relief from tight money is unlikely to be of more than intermittent help to a region like the Atlantic provinces. If the grounds on which such relief is claimed are the unemployment and underemployment of manpower, and if these are not intermittent but chronic, then the action called for should be designed to remove the underemployment progressively and should not be limited to providing temporary relief, any more than one should treat toothache with an occasional aspirin.
Mr. Cairncross came to the conclusion that bank finance alone was not regarded as one of the major obstacles to economic growth in the Atlantic provinces and that it has not been a major factor in the fluctuations in activity in that particular region. In fact he went even further when he declared that whatever the conceivable effects, the real effects of credit restriction within the region appear to have been far less conspicuous than the damping effects of credit restrictions outside the region and of obstacles to expansion in other markets. This, again, is very significant to the situation we have to face today in the Atlantic provinces.
In other words, he said the existing monetary policy in its general application was detrimental to the economy of the Atlantic region and contributed in no uncertain terms in creating a contraction in markets which was reflected largely in areas which already operated under unfavourable conditions.
Mr. Cairncross made it very clear and significant that he could see no way of keeping interest rates on private loans in the Atlantic provinces below the rates obtainable on comparable loans elsewhere. But he did not hesitate to suggest that loans from public bodies were quite another matter and this did not prevent such agencies as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation relieving existing shortages by allowing the building industry more leeway and offering special help where it was most needed. He did not hesitate to suggest that such agencies as the industrial development bank could apply special or preferred policies to the Atlantic region.
I know that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming), who was one of the Atlantic premiers who asked for the services of Mr. Cairncross, would be interested in expressing his opinion and showing his influence with the present government so that some of the recommendations made in this report could now be implemented to the advantage of the Atlantic provinces.

He proposed that the taxpayer would have the option of writing off these expenses on the basis of double depreciation in any one of the first three years. I heard the Minister of Labour say earlier tonight that municipalities did not want to be classified as being distressed areas. A number of these newspapers are alwoys on the side of this government whenever that is possible, but apparently that is not possible in so far as this issue is concerned. The Toronto Globe and Mail of March 6, 1961, says, "No solution here". The article continues:
The old saying about a mountain labouring and bringing forth a mouse applies to the dominion government's proposals for aiding depressed areas as outlined in the House of Commons this week by Labour Minister Michael Starr. They constitute a poorly thought out and thoroughly inadequate approach to a serious problem.
It might have been thought that any such program would begin by naming the districts or communities which the cabinet considered to be in need of special help. But Mr. Starr indicates that the government would not designate particular areas. The local authorities would have to establish, to the cabinet's satisfaction, that their communities were economically sick.
I could continue quoting from these newspaper articles. Even the Ottawa Journal says that the government has sidestepped naming Canada's depressed areas. Similar articles have appeared in the Financial Post, the Financial Times and the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. The Halifax newspaper, which I believe supports this government, terms this a debilitated program, and I think that comment is aptly worded.
Earlier today my leader put on the record a six-point program designed to help these areas of chronic unemployment. I would predict that by tomorrow the cabinet ministers will be saying they have never heard anything about it.
In the few minutes I have left, I should like to refer to my own area. Some municipalities in my area want to know whether they can qualify under this plan for double depreciation. There are many unemployed in the city of Welland, in Port Colborne and in the Thorold area. I do not have the precise figures, but over the week end I was told there were approximately 3,000 unemployed in the city of Welland. This is quite a large number. Many young people who have just entered the labour market have been unable to get work. Industries have been cutting back their labour forces. This cut-back has been the result of automation as well as a lowering of the demand for production. These industries have been unable to sell their products. One result has been that the workers in the 40 to 45 age group have been thrown out of work.
The men in this age group cannot secure new employment because of their age. Even if a new industry were established in these areas, the men in this age group would still find it difficult to get work. I have referred

before to the fact that the pension plans in many of these plants militate against older men securing employment. I believe these remarks would apply to any new plants that might be established under this double depreciation plan now proposed by the government. Even if a man in the 40 to 45 age group did take vocational training, he would still face the problem of age when he sought new employment. I think something should be done to cope with this problem. These remarks might not be quite in order, Mr. Speaker, but this is a factor in the unemployment in my area and in several other areas. Many of these people become unemployed after reaching 40, and that is the very worst time in their lives for this to happen. I feel that the government should give some consideration to this group of older workers.
I have often said in the house that something could be done through the provisions of the Income Tax Act. I think the government could provide earlier vesting in pension funds by withholding in whole or in part the right to exemptions which is allowed under the Income Tax Act. If this were done it would contribute a great deal toward helping people to find jobs. Certainly in our area a number of people have run out of unemployment insurance benefits. If a new factory were established in that area, it would help the young people. However, as I said before, you would still have the problem of the older workers. While I might be out of order, I should like to bring this problem of the older workers to the attention of the government at this time.
Some question has been raised as to whether or not the people in these areas are actually hungry. In passing, I might say that three Toronto newspapers have said there are hungry children in Toronto. During the consideration of the departmental estimates, I should like to say a word about nutrition. I think that if the government did nothing in addition to what they are now doing except to see to it that the children and others were properly nourished, they would have taken an important step at this time.
Over the week end I was talking with some officials in Welland who did not think the present regulations would allow double depreciation to the plants in Welland if they proceeded to make new products. I was informed in Welland-and I do not know whether it is so-that Welland stands second to Peterborough with the largest number of people per capita on the relief rolls in Ontario.
The government has advertised this scheme as a stimulant to our economy but I say that

it is too restrictive and inflexible to be anything of the kind. This is further evidence in my opinion that the government is giving no serious consideration to the problem of unemployment. We heard the Minister of Finance say not long ago that there was no emergency in respect of unemployment. When I heard the Minister of Finance make that remark, and when I looked at these measures brought forward by the government, I came to the conclusion that the government is not taking the matter of unemployment very seriously at all.
We heard the Minister of Labour announce the criteria the municipalities would have to meet before they could be classified as surplus manpower areas. I suggest that announcement is the biggest farce that I have ever heard in this House of Commons. According to the explanatory memorandum of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as tabled here not long ago, these areas will be eligible, under certain regulations, to be declared as surplus manpower areas by the governor in council. Municipalities must apply on certain prescribed forms and the Department of Trade and Commerce will then decide whether they are eligible as areas for double depreciation. These regulations, as I said, must be complied with in order that the governor in council can name a municipality as a surplus manpower area entitled to the double depreciation. I would appeal to the government to give to the criteria a more generous interpretation than they have indicated will be given so far in this debate.
I think it is natural that the people in my riding of Welland would be very happy indeed to have a new industry established there. I feel that this would certainly allow many of the young people to go to work and would, I hope, as well provide jobs for the older unemployed workers. I would again appeal to the government on behalf of the older workers for the establishment of a portable pension. I might suggest that no matter what trade an older man took up he would still be faced with the problem regarding his age; and he would certainly benefit greatly by the establishment of a portable pension which, as the Minister of Finance has said, could be easily done through the provisions of the Income Tax Act. If this were done I feel that many of these people would be able to continue working rather than be forced to lead lives of uncertainty, as they are bound to do for the rest of their lives without it.
